utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A slight procedural matter before we begin today. I was told that some confidential information was revealed through our redaction order, so I hereby -- the Chamber directs the Registry to reclassify the public redaction order filed on 23rd of April, 2010, with page number D34952 as a confidential document in order to protect the identity of the witness concerned. Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. I would just like to take care of two housekeeping matters, very briefly, if you don't mind. This one document, D77, which was an MFI document because the translation had not been attached, the translation is now there and I've been told that it's necessary for me to make an oral application to now turn this into an admitted exhibit. It's number D77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Secondly, during the testimony of Ambassador Okun, it was indicated that a letter had been sent concerning the shelling of the Sarajevo Hospital, and with the assistance of the Prosecution we did locate a letter from General Morillon to President Izetbegovic, and we would ask that that letter be admitted. We've discussed this with the Prosecution, and they don't have any objection. It's in e-court as 1D900. We would ask that it be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D900. If you could remind me whether that letter was dealt with yesterday, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was mentioned, actually, I believe, the day before yesterday. It was part of the supplemental information that Ambassador Okun had provided to the Prosecutor upon his arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Robinson indicated, we don't object to the admission of that letter. There's not a representation that that specific letter was referred to in the testimony, but the issues connected with that letter, as Mr. Robinson indicated, were, indeed, addressed, and we have no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Both of the documents are admitted. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. We'll give the exhibit number to the last item.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D900 will be Exhibit D99.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to Your Excellencies and to you, Mr. Ambassador, and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, before I pick up from where we left off yesterday, I'd like to ask you this: Did you have a chance to read something from the extensive diary of Professor Koljevic? I'm sure you know that he left behind him a very precisely-written diary with entries -- with daily entries.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we have time, we'll come back to that. But since you say you haven't read it, then it's not a priority. I'd like to call up on e-court next 1D217 now, please. 1D217. All we need is the English version. May we zoom in to the English version, please. We don't need the other one. Mr. Ambassador, there's been a lot of correspondence between -- there was a lot of correspondence between us and the Red Cross. Now, this is one of my letters to the Prime Minister Branko Djeric, who says -- and it says: "Respected President, I'm enclosing copies of the reports I just received regarding the state of the prisons of Manjaca and Bileca. In relation to these reports, I sent a letter to Mr. Cornelius Sommaruga, the president of the ICRC, and General Ratko Mladic. "I expect that the government, through the ministries of Law and Internal Affairs, based on these reports, take immediate measures for the improvement of the living conditions in the jails that are operated by civilian authorities on our territory." Now, did you know about this, that this was something we dealt with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, from the International Committee of the Red Cross, that they were in touch with you in connection with their desire that the condition in the detention camps be improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have 1D244, please. I'd like to tender that previous document, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have an order to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska, the ministry -- just a moment. Let me remind you that the previous document was dated the 7th of August, 1992, and the date of this document is the 19th of August, 1992. And we were in the full throes of co-operation, working on the Vance-Owen Plan. Now, the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska to the Ministry of the Interior, to all centres -- to all the security service centres. And you know that these centres provided for a number of neighbouring centres. You know that, I assume. And then it says: "According to our act of the 13th of June, 1992, in respect -- respect for international norms of war, once again," and I'd like to stress that I said "once again," "I hereby order: "That all entities honour their commitment to comply with the International Humanitarian Law, especially the 3rd and the 4th Geneva Conventions. "2. To issue instructions to all combatants and all employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to respect imprisoned individuals, civilians, medical institutions, private and public places, the emblem of the Red Cross Red Cross, and the people and resources of the United Nations. "3," we're going to come back to that, "To prevent the forced resettlement and the taking of other illegal actions against the civilian population, and the possible confirmation of selling the property or statement that the refugees will not return, have no legality and are declared null and void. "4. To immediately take steps to improve conditions in all prisons within the Serbian Republic, in accordance with the recommendations given by the International Red Cross, during its visits to those places. In accordance with the previous decision, all prisoners of war who are ill and will not become members of enemy armies should be released immediately. "5. To immediately notify the International Red Cross about the state of all prisons within the Serbian Republic, and to provide accurate lists to this organisation of people held in those prisons." And now we come to number 6, although it says "5": "All members of the Army and police of the Serbian Republic are obliged to provide every assistance to members of the International Red Cross and the High Commissioner for Refugees to the United Nations and other humanitarian organisations." And then the general position reads as follows: "Every organs of the army and police in the area of responsibility is obliged to carry out a vigorous investigation of any suspicion or sign of violation of International Humanitarian Laws." Now, did you know that we repeated several times, up until the 19th of August, 1992, express orders that were never rescinded and withdrawn, instructing the authorities how they must behave towards civilians, prisoners of war, international organisations, and the like?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware from ICRC directly about their -- about their communications with you, as I just mentioned. They also made us aware that the conditions in the camps did not improve, as Dr. Sommaruga stated in his speech of August 26, 1992, at the London Conference. But your letter that you just read is certainly commendable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just put you right? This is an order. I didn't send the army letters. I sent orders to the army and the police. Thank you. Now, may this document be tendered into evidence. 1D244 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no objection. I just wanted to note that this bears, in the English translation, the heading of "Defence translation," and this is a previously-translated document. It appears in the Prosecution's 65 ter list, and I even believe it's a previous exhibit. But, in any event, I only mention that because there was mention made of limited translation resources, and so I would encourage the review of documents about to be translated to see if, in fact, it's already been accomplished. But there's no objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there -- I wonder if there's a regime through which the Defence team can know whether some documents were already translated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It would have been uploaded in e-court, part of the 65 ter list, I think -- I accept the fact that there may be some documents for which some additional inquiry might be made. I think this is one that just might have slipped through the cracks, and it's not -- it's no matter of finger-pointing, but I think in the interests of mutual efficient use of resources, it needed to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted as number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, the next document I'd like called up on e-court is 1D312, 312.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Ambassador, let me tell you what it's about. As we said before the war that law and order was in our hands and that chaos was in nobody's hands, there were killings, and here's how the state organs acted if they learnt of something like that. This is dated the same day as the previous document, the 19th of August, 1992, to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic: "There are indications that in the village of Bastezi, at Celinac, five Muslim civilians were killed. "I hereby order the most thorough investigation to be conducted, criminals to be identified and brought to justice. "Ministry officials from the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka, the Station of Public Security Celinac, must take all measures to protect the Muslim civilian population of Celinac municipality, which, according to our knowledge, has no military organisation, neither is prepared for military intervention against the Serbian people." Mr. Ambassador, if something similar were to happen, for example, in your country, I'm sure that from a central level, somebody would show interest or order the FBI to intervene; isn't the that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We consider it to be what you call a federal case in America. Now, what I want to ask you is this, Mr. Ambassador: Did any of your associates tell you that General Galic informed -- gave out information that by September 1992, there were 6.300 criminal reports filed, mostly from the military domain, but from other areas, too, and that Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of police of that general area, informed people that there were two and a half to 3.000 criminal reports filed? They informed us of this and requested that the judiciary should step up its work, that the court authorities were lagging behind. Now, did they inform you -- did you know about this number of criminal reports, and trials are still going on in Bosnia based on those criminal reports filed at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we knew of the specific number. We were aware of the interchanges of all parties with their subordinates. And it is also to be noted that we had no capacity to check on whether these orders were ever carried out by the local police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for 1D235, 235, the next document to be called up, please, let's just reinforce what you just said, Mr. Ambassador. The Serbs were really rather weak in their propaganda, in advertising, so that these things during the war passed unnoticed, really. And that's our mistake, but we felt that it wasn't in good taste for us to publish the steps we were duty-bound to take anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think your statement warrants an answer from the ambassador, if he so wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have nothing to say on that. It certainly was not in good taste to ethnically cleanse people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you do not object to the order to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it will be admitted as D102?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D235 is the next document. It is a letter to the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, to Mico Stanisic, the minister of police, and to Momcilo Mandic, justice minister. And the date is the 22nd of October, 1992, and we're still together -- you are still with us in our crisis: "Gentlemen. As you know, I have in the past signed an official authorisation to the representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross, on the basis of which they must be allowed, in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, unfettered access to prisons and prisoners. I am sending you, again, a copy of this authorisation. "I have been informed that some local police, military, and civilian authorities are completely ignoring this document and are obstructing the normal work of the representatives of the International Committee. "I urgently demand that you immediately inform all your subordinate officers that the authorisation for the International Red Cross Committee representatives affixed with my signature must absolute be respected. "I shall order a thorough investigation in all cases of failure to comply with this demand." Now, Mr. Ambassador, let me ask you this: Although the Republika Srpska and the United States of America cannot really be compared, does your president have any separate organs or does he have to go through the official organs in requesting that the law be complied with? Does he have direct connection with the local level or does he have to issue orders and contact the central level of government.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would go through a regular procedure, not direct, but indirect, as you indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me ask you this: Does the president of the United States, outside these structures, does it have some bodies of investigation within his cabinet, for example?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does. As you mentioned previously, there is the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the president of the United States is, under our Constitution, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, so his wishes in that regard are automatically obeyed by all military units at every level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I did believe that that was so. I assumed that that was so. But outside those structures, he doesn't have a secret police, for example, of which nobody knows anything about, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly does not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, Your Excellencies, I'd like to tender this document, 1D235, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document I'd like called up on e-court is 1D253.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, 1D253, let me inform you, Mr. Ambassador, what the document is about. The date now is the 11th of March, 1993. We're still together, you're still at our conference, until, I believe it was, mid-May 1993, wasn't it? Now, this is a directive. The president of the republic issues the following directive to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which we had from the autumn of 1992, we had Republika Srpska. Now, the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army is obliged to continue, in future, the following: "1. To enable the undisturbed passage and protection of mail, equipment, and personnel who render assistance intended for the civilian population of the opposite side." Now, 2 is: "To prohibit any misuse, for military purposes, of food supplies, crops, plumbing and drinking water reservoirs, and water dams." And number 3, it says: "To abide by the Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of war and their protocols, 1 and 2, as well as The Hague Convention on the Laws and Customs of War -- Ground War from 1907, and other provisions of International War Law, and; "4. To ensure that all army units make themselves acquainted with this direction and to sustain it, enforce it." You know that on the 13th of June, 1992, we issued basic instructions and extensive instructions about this, applying to prisoners of war and conduct with prisoners of war, and now this is underlined and emphasised once again in March because, as we know, in the chaos of a civil war, arbitrary behaviour can come about. So this is to restrict that arbitrary behaviour and to ensure that everything functions properly. Do you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were aware of this general directive. It was an important issue because this praiseworthy directive was not observed, neither by the Bosnian Serb Army, nor by the other armies. Food convoys under the protection -- or perhaps I should say accompanied by UNPROFOR troops were routinely stopped, robbed, made to pay money to get through certain check-points. So while this directive is certainly praiseworthy, it has to be noted that it was observed in the breach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ambassador, do you know of a single case whereby the Serb Army or the Serb police asked for money for the passage of convoys, free passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many cases. You will find them in the UNPROFOR records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, could the Prosecution provide us with that evidence then in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, do you know how many convoys passed through and how many convoys encountered problems along the way? And I say that it is less than 1 per cent, and perhaps an even smaller number than that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not accurately put a number on it, except to repeat that UNPROFOR told us, on more than one occasion, that the convoys were being routinely disturbed by all parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will confirm, Mr. Ambassador, that checks were enforced and we issued instructions about how these convoys should be checked and examined, and do you agree that there was abuse in the use of convoys; taking supplies to our adversaries, for example?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was abuse on all parties:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 1D274 now, please. While we're waiting for it, I would like us to clarify a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there smuggling of war material? Was there abuse of that kind in humanitarian aid convoys which made it incumbent upon us to carry out routine checks of the content of the vehicles in these convoys? Was ammunition, weapons, and the like found?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that for a fact, but I can imagine it to be the case. I have already testified that, for example, President Tudjman escorted me once to the Zagreb Airport, where he took us through a plane from Iran. It was an Iran Air commercial 747 that had military supplies for the Bosnian Muslim Army. They were mostly gas masks, however, which were not useful, but they were military supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we were more worried about gas masks than uniforms. We don't mind if they are not dressed properly. However, if they are ordering gas masks, then they're planning on using poisonous gas and the like. So that is what I'd like to say in this regard. And could we now have 174, please -- 274. While we're waiting, Mr. Ambassador, do you remember that I asked a very high-ranking official of Republika Srpska, Professor Koljevic, to chair the committee for co-operating with the United Nations, so that he could intervene from that very high level, even when I was not there, in order to improve the situation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that Mr. Professor Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik took charge of your affairs at the conference when you were not present. I was never made aware of the specific instructions you gave Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the number I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, the previous document, 253, will be admitted, unless there's objection, as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D104, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is from the 7th of May. It is being sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The president of the republic is passing the following decision: "1. Stop immediately with all military offensive activities. "2. In case of the enemy attack on positions of Republika Srpska, offer resistance," et cetera. 3 is noteworthy with regard to this topic: "Enable undisturbed distribution of humanitarian aid to areas of the opposite side. Check the humanitarian aid completely, efficiently, with as little delay as possible and in a fair way. For this task, immediately train the necessary personnel from the military police and police and facilitate them with necessary resources for carrying out their work. "Facilitate compliance with UN Resolution 824, and concrete measures are to be agreed upon through negotiations." This is yet another one of the many orders issued to the military so that they could carry out, as specifically as possible, their tasks based on the commitments that we undertook. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the conclusion I come -- from the multiplicity of orders, directives, instructions, letters that you sent on this subject to your military, from that I conclude that they were not being followed. If they were listening to you, you would not have had to send so many orders. So apparently the orders, while praiseworthy in themselves, were not being observed by your troops in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I have 1D256, please. In the meantime, I would like to inform you - I don't know whether you knew about that - that I always took into account the observations made by representatives of the international community, and I often accused my own military officers on the basis of these allegations, and very often these allegations proved to be untrue. So sometimes I attacked them for no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were such cases as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could imagine there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please have a number for the previous document, and now I'm asking for 256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 274 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D105, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're dealing with the 12th of May, 1993. The Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. It's being sent to Mr. Ratko Adzic, the minister: "On the basis of the Constitution of Republika Srpska, I hereby order that all places of worship in the town and its surroundings be secured and protected from increased terrorist activity by means of reinforced Banja Luka Security Services Centre patrols. "Execute this order immediately and report the measures undertaken to me." Did anybody report that to you, that we took place of religious places, places of worship?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew of the -- we knew of the bad situation in Banja Luka. Churches were being destroyed, mosques were being destroyed by Serbian forces. And you will recall, Dr. Karadzic, that because of that, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen asked that you allow them to go to Banja Luka to seek to prevent the wanton destruction of these Christian and Muslim religious buildings, and you did give them that permission. They went there with your acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I actually have that particular piece of news. We received this from the Prosecution, so could it please be put on the overhead projector, but it could be zoomed in. It's in English. You are right, but there is something I'd like to add. I asked Mr. Vance and Lord Owen to come to Banja Luka. They did come at my invitation, and I met them in Gradiska, at the border crossing there.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It is noted in my journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We used to call this machine "Episcope" a long time ago, although now it is called "Graphiscope." For the time being, the document is not on the list. Yes, that's it. Could it be enlarged a bit more, please. Thank you: [In English] "Banja Luka, September 15. "Bosnian Serb leader expects co-chairmen of Conference on Yugoslavia to dismiss allegations about ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka. Bosnia-Herzegovina Serb leader Radovan Karadzic Friday said he was confident that the co-chairman of the Conference of Yugoslavia, Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, would disprove allegations about the existence of ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka, a town in Bosnia controlled by Bosnian Serbs. Vance and Owen arrived in Banja Luka on Friday and met with representatives of the town's Muslims and Croats. Vance and Owen can see for themselves that there exists no discrimination against the Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka, Karadzic said at a news conference held in the town. He added that believed the co-chairmen to be impartial. "Stressing that he was against all forms of forcible expulsion, Karadzic said that owing to the war, itself, many Serbs, Croats, and Muslims were leaving their areas." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Ambassador, I would like us to clear up a matter. It seems, on the basis of your explanation, that we did not deny that we were doing this, whereas Mr. Tieger very skillfully alleged, during his direct examination, that I had agreed that my forces were carrying out ethnic cleansing. What I am saying here now is that we could understand that there might be fear and departures from zones where people were a minority to zones where they were a majority. I forecast that in the speech made on the 25th of January that we looked at yesterday. Here, you see that we have constantly denied that it was the state organs that were forcefully or forcibly expelling the population or doing anything of that regard. Do you see now, Ambassador, that we denied this, that the state, indeed, had nothing to do with this; however, the phenomenon, itself, was there, and I had even forecast that before the war? Anyone can forecast that kind of thing can happen during a civil war. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I heard that only in Serbo-Croatian, and now I'll have to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please take your time to read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that you didn't receive the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll be quick. I know time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The point is that we did deny that it was the state that was carrying out ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, in answer to your question, I must report that I had extensive discussions with Secretary Vance when he returned from Banja Luka, and his report to me was not in accord with what you said. He had seen intense destruction of Muslim and Christian shrines and came away with the impression that the expulsion and the intimidation of the Croat and Muslim people in Banja Luka was an organised affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, we never received such information from Mr. Vance, either in writing or orally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted or at least marked for identification, Excellency? Actually, we have it because it was the ambassador that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 256, before that, will be admitted, and as ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. 256, I was going to ask if that could be MFI'd. I wanted to do some checking on the provenance of that before admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 256 is his order that we saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to check with the Defence and perhaps other ways, just a quick check on the provenance of that document before it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "provenance"? It's his order, and -- do we have its original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly right. I'd like to know how it was obtained, from what sources. And I appreciate, on its face, that it's an order of a particular date. That may not present any problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need to come back to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly I would get back to the Court by the next court date, which I guess is next week, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before we come to -- could you tell me what it is about the document we saw through the ELMO? Is it a news clipping or -- Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish, Excellency. This is a review, a survey of news agency news that came in on that day. The OTP has a collection of such reviews, and I received it from them under that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I believe, if I saw that correctly, it was part of a "Tanjug" excerpt. In any event, I don't have any objection to the admission of that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D107, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding was that it was not listed in the 65 ter list, and then you also requested the addition of it to the list. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Excellency. I actually refrained from proffering it too soon, but the ambassador spoke about Banja Luka and I wanted to show this in order to jog the ambassador's memory in terms of what happened when Mr. Vance and Lord Owen came to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, I don't -- it seems to me that this was not something that was held back in any way. It arose in the context that the accused mentioned, and I have no objection to its -- to an oral motion to add to it as proffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like to ask for 1D258 in e-court, please. Is it the 12th? No. This is in the Serbian language. Could we please have it in English for the benefit of the others in the courtroom? Thank you. I'll read the Serbian version, but could we have the English version for the benefit of all others in the courtroom. 1D258 is the English version. If it hasn't been translated, allow me to read it, and then we are going to provide a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 9th of June, 1993: "I hereby order to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska: "1. Soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council who sought shelter from Serb territory in Vlasic should be transported in an organised fashion, along with all their weaponry, to Vares." You remember that 10.000 civilians and all soldiers fled from Travnik after an attack by the Muslim Army. They fled to Vlasic, the Serb territory, and this pertains to that: "2. As for Croatian civilians who fled to Serb territory, they should be allowed to go to Herceg-Bosna or the Republic of Croatia, as they wish. "3. This should be carried out straight away, and report back to me on the outcome." May I remind you that Croatian civilians at the time often said, "Big deal, UNPROFOR. For us, the Serb Army is UNPROFOR." Do you know that we took in an enormous number of Croatians who had fled, we took them in in our territory, and we let them to go wherever they wanted to go? We actually have a translation on the ELMO, so could all others in the court have access to it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ambassador. Did you know --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that connection, Dr. Karadzic, I was not aware. By June 9, 1993, Secretary Vance and I had ceased our activity in Bosnia and were directing our attention, at the instruction of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, towards the Greek-Macedonian dispute. But I see this document, and I can well believe that it's accurate, because as I have testified previously, and indeed as is widely known, in many respects the Bosnian Serb Army and the Croatian Army co-operated against the Muslims, as, indeed, the leaders also co-operated from time to time. This period, the spring and summer of 1993, saw intense fighting between Bosnian Croat forces, on the one side, and Bosnian Muslim forces, on the other, so it is not surprising that the Bosnian Serb Army was told to help the Bosnian Croat soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I would like to remind you that -- and, actually, I believe you know about this - that from a religious point of view, we are closer to the Croats, but in ethnic terms, we thought that the Muslims were closer to us because we thought that they were Serbs - that's what most Serbs believe, anyway - who converted to Islam against their own will. But why would there not be Serbs, ethnic Serbs, of all three or four faiths? Croats are Christians, like we are, but ethnically we consider the Muslims to be totally identical to Serbs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no question that you believed that, and I was aware of it at the time. It should also be noted that the Croatians make the same argument, that the Bosnian Muslims were Croats that -- who had been converted to Islam after the Turkish conquest of Bosnia. President Tudjman made that point. Mate Boban made that point repeatedly. Indeed, President Tudjman made the point -- the additional point that it was precisely because Bosnian-Herzegovinian Muslims were really Croatians that during World War II Bosnia and Herzegovina had been given to Croatia, it was a part of Croatia. So it is correct, Dr. Karadzic, to say that the Bosnian Serbs regarded the Muslims as originally Serbs, and it's also correct to say that the Croatians regarded the Bosnian Muslims as originally Croatians. It also should be added that there was much intermarriage particularly between Serb and Muslim, and also, but to a lesser degree, between the Roman Catholic Croatians and Muslims. I think the basic point on all of this is that, indeed, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic/multi-religious state in which the groups lived peacefully until 1991. Could I have this printed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could 258 please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused referred to a translation of this document, which I didn't receive and didn't see on the screen. That's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I would just ask that it be -- two minor things, then. I would ask, to the extent that can be provided early, that would be helpful. Secondly, it seems to me it might be a preferable practice, if there is an English translation, for the -- when a document -- when there is reading of a document for which there is an English translation, that we read from the translation rather than from the original. Otherwise, we have two translations of the document; one, the English that is submitted, and, two, the one that's contemporaneous in court. So I only -- I raise that to the Court. I think that's the way it's typically dealt with. The Court may have something different in mind, but I wanted to note that issue doesn't need to be resolved at the moment. I know we are pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's inevitable when the accused is reading from the B/C/S version, then the translation, which might be a bit different from the English translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which is why, I think in other Chambers, we've been encouraged to read from the translation that's been submitted. But, again, I only raise that as a matter that can -- that may be an issue and, in any event, can be dealt with when we have a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. No objection to the admission, in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that we did e-mail this translation, that my team e-mailed it. These are translations that are arriving from elsewhere, because the archives were destroyed when all of this happened. It was given to the OTP in 1997 and 1998, without any impediments whatsoever, believing that these are investigators of the Tribunal, not of the OTP. They were given these documents twice, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador -- well, may we have 1D221 displayed next, please, on e-court. And while we're waiting for that, Mr. Ambassador, do you know of a manifest of ours of the 21st of August, 1992, when we determined our position in a document that was called "We accept/we propose/we shall carry out"? It will come up on our screens in just a moment. "We accept/we propose/we shall do," and there we let the international representatives know how they can count on us in their co-operation with us, what they can count on. Do you see that? It's on our screens. Now, at that time you were deep in -- well, not "deep." You arrived one week later and were thrown into the midst of our crisis. But, anyway, I'd like to draw your attention to this document. It says: "We accept to form, together with the other two national communities, the community of states of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the existing external borders. "We accept that the territorial issues be resolved within the framework of the conference initiated by the European Community." And it was still Carrington's conference: "We shall not accept territorial claims by neighbouring countries, if there are any." And then under "We propose," it says the following: "We propose an absolute cease-fire and the signing of a truce with UNPROFOR supervision. "We propose signing an agreement on the free return of refugees, the free circulation of civilians, with full guarantee of human and proper rights. "We propose immediate bilateral and trilateral talks between the representatives of all three national communities concerning all issues." And then under the heading, "We shall do": "We shall make possible for all humanitarian convoys to move freely to all directions and shall give guarantees for their safety over all Serb territories. "We shall prevent ethnic cleansing. "We shall carry out investigations into all cases where forceful transfer of civilian population and suspected -- and shall punish all responsible persons. "Any documents on selling or giving up of property, made under duress, will be declared null and void and without any validity. "We are ready to exchange all prisoners of war on the 'all for all' basis and shall close all prisons." Now, Mr. Ambassador, is this a fair offer?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This offer was made a few days before the London Conference opened. We were, of course, aware of it. It was made in the obvious attempt to put a good face on the actions, the ethnic cleansing, the deportations, the expulsions, that were largely being taken by Bosnian Serb forces. We were always aware of the offer, for example, to exchange prisoners on an "all for all" basis. Dr. Karadzic made that offer directly to the International Conference. The general picture, with relation to this document, was given most clearly five days later by President Sommaruga of the ICRC. That document has already been discussed and introduced to the Court. And he gives a totally different picture of the situation on the ground. But I have no doubt that this document, as I say, was presented at the London Conference in order to put a good face on the situation which, in reality, was quite different. With respect to another item, to propose a cease-fire and the signing of the truce, we've discussed that several times in the court. Since the Bosnian Serb armies at this point controlled approximately 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was, of course, in their interest that the fighting stop while they were way ahead, and they repeatedly offered to stop fighting. They never offered to retreat from their gains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that will be given a response.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the meantime, may we have 1D288, dated the 22nd of April, 1992. I have to put that to the Court, in view of your answer. But in the meantime, may we get a number -- be given a number for this 221 document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D109.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for 1D288, the next document that I'd like us to look at, Mr. Ambassador, I'd like to remind you that at all times we envisaged that we would come down to 53 per cent, because we always accepted the fact that the Muslims would have 30 per cent and the Croats 17 per cent. That was confirmed in all plans. But I always said that there was no chance of us withdrawing until peace was signed and guaranteed, because then we would lose the war. We couldn't withdraw from strategically-advantageous positions, and I'm sure you'll agree. Now, this next document is the platform which I proposed, still as party president, without any state function, and the date of that is the 22nd of April, 1992. So I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "Platform offered by Radovan Karadzic for solving the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "1. Unconditional and immediate cease-fire and respect for the April the 4th, 1992 agreement. "2. Urgent continuation of the Conference on B and H and its continuing work until reaching final solution. "3. Under the Conference on BH, priority given to making maps of the city of Sarajevo and of its constituent states. "4. Public commitment by all sides in B and H that the constituent parts will not be annexed to the neighbouring states and that armed forces out of Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be sent for or accepted. "5. Public commitment by all sides in B and H that the policy of an accomplished act," fait accompli, "even the one originated from the Communist heritage, will not be accepted, and territorial advantages gained through the use of force will not be recognised. "Urgent application of constitutional agreements," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, this was two weeks after the outset of the war, a little over a fortnight. Now, were you aware of this, and is this a fair offer made on time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Bosnia on April 22 and was not aware of this document. I should note that the third point refers to what we've discussed earlier; namely, the desire of the Bosnian Serbs to partition Sarajevo. And so it's consistent with that known position. And I should also mention that April 22 is about 10 days after the Bosnian Serb artillery started shelling Sarajevo. And this, on its face, seems to me a reasonable offer. How it was accepted by people who were being shelled mercilessly in Sarajevo is, of course, another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Let me just remind you. On the 22nd of April, there was no Army of Republika Srpska. Right up until the 20th of May, it was the JNA Army. Now, after that -- furthermore, let me say on the 22nd of April, the Serb side did not control 70 per cent, and we didn't know who controlled what percentage of anything. And then the proposal that is made is that the municipalities, the opstina, be freely formed in Sarajevo, without dividing the town, and we have permanent public comparison between Sarajevo and Brussels. Of all the municipalities in Brussels, none of them are mixed. Gerrymandering was carried out of the municipalities in Sarajevo to make the Serbs the minority in most of those municipalities, and those are the facts. And there would be no wolves [as interpreted] in the town, because on the 22nd of April we still hoped that there would be no war. Do you agree -- do you agree that on the 22nd of April, we could have thought that there would not -- it would not come to war and that the Army of Republika Srpska did not exist at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is correct, and I apologise for using the word "army" of Bosnia because the JNA did exist on April 22nd. It became the army of the Bosnian Serbs a few weeks later in May, as Dr. Karadzic has said. The military situation in April, though, was mis-described by Dr. Karadzic, because, in fact, the fighting began in March, not in April. I was in Sarajevo and Bosnia at the very time, wearing a flak-jacket and looking rather awkward with a helmet, but I remember very clearly the fighting that began in March. So by April, it was pretty well advanced. The full force of war had not been unleashed in Bosnia, but it was serious fighting, something like September 1939 in Europe, not -- you know, the French invasion, not the Soviet invasion by Russia, but there was serious fighting at the same time. And, as I say, the guns were already on the hills surrounding Sarajevo, and the city was being pounded with artillery. The siege of Sarajevo, which the Bosnian Serbs always denied was a siege, but was, in fact, a siege, was becoming a fact of life. So hostilities were pretty well advanced by April 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Well, you're forcing me to expand the topic, but let me tell you this: Up until the 1st of April, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was only the Croatian and Muslim parties that were attacking and killing Serbs, but -- and then the 25th and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly slow down, please, for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to follow you because you spoke too fast. So could you kindly repeat your previous question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: Do you challenge the fact that up until the 1st of April, in March, the attacks were solely conducted by the Croatian and Muslim forces, Croatian forces from Croatian even, and that in March, there was no shelling in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks in March were primarily Bosnian Serb attacks against the Muslims. I was in Sarajevo and able to observe it in Sarajevo myself. It is true that the Croatian Army also entered Bosnia in March at Bosanski Brod, and this was well known. It is not true that attacks were made in any number by the Muslim forces against the Bosnian Serb or the JNA, because the fact is the Muslims had no army and were merely in the process of organising themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll prove that very easily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Excellencies, I'd like to tender this document 288 into evidence. I didn't think I would be dealing with it today, but I've been brought into that situation. It was confirmed by the witness, and it was a platform that was generally known of the 20th of April -- 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As the accused has indicated, it was not a document that was noticed. However, we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Addition to the list is granted, and it will be admitted into exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D110, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this now -- well, that was -- 211, was that admitted into evidence, 211? Yes, I'm told it has. May we have 1D853 called up next, please. While we're waiting for that, Mr. Ambassador, I'd like to draw the Court's attention to the position taken by the state organs of Republika Srpska, stating that nothing that was a war option was an acceptable option and that there was no fait accompli. And here we have an instruction of the 23rd of August, 1992. We have the original somewhere as well. But this is a set of instructions, and I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "Instructions to all presidents of municipalities. "It has become common for local people to move into empty flats instead of refugees, and they sometimes even retain some kind of 'right' for several flats. "The occurrence or issue of abandoned flats is a war issue, and so are the refugees. This means that both occurrences are temporary. "Please strictly observe the following instructions: "1. Temporarily-abandoned flats can be given for temporary use to refugees only, not to local people. "2. Accurate records are to be kept on both the temporarily-abandoned flats and the refugees. The temporarily-abandoned flats can be given for use by a commission only, which issues the decision on the temporary use. "3. Any abuse, nepotism, and failure to observe these instructions entails not only political responsibility, but also criminal prosecution. "In addition to legal obligations regarding conduct, you must display political awareness and the tact that dealing with the refugees, their accommodation and employment, as is required in you by the programme or the party that has brought you to office." [Interpretation] The original exists, too, somewhere. But I'd like to remind you, Mr. Ambassador, that the government, in April, forbid the trafficking of property while the war was on, and that with this document the Presidency prohibited the use of abandoned property by the local population so that that should not become a motive for which to exert pressure on neighbours -- Muslim and Croatian neighbours to leave. Did you know about this set of instructions?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I do recall our discussion, Dr. Karadzic, yours and mine, on the question of apartments, in which you told me that the war began when you were expelled from your flat in Sarajevo. And this document is certainly a worthy document, in and of itself. As I've mentioned in connection with the other documents, all praiseworthy, they would not have been issued had there not been a need for them to be issued. And it is certainly welcome to see now that the intentions of the Presidency were good. It's a great pity that the reality was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's true, there were occurrences of that kind, and that is precisely why these instructions were issued, and people were also punished. But practice generally needs laws and regulations to see that the laws are implemented, so new provisions are need to do prevent anything like this. I'd like to tender 1D853. The original is on e-court, but we have just displayed the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the meantime, before we dealt with this document you mentioned 1D211, but I don't have a recollection we admitted that into evidence. With that, we'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 221, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have a translation for MFI 97. I would advise that that can be admitted as D97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that we are missing a Court Reporter now, so I don't think we can proceed. Okay. Mr. Robinson, could you kindly repeat your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm advised that we have the translation for MFI 97, and I would ask that be admitted as D97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have called up on e-court D101, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, we already had this document. The date is the 19th of August, a week before you arrived. Now, I'd just like to draw your attention to point 3 there, point 3 of this order, which reads as follows: "According to our act of the 13th of June, to prevent the forced resettlement and taking other illegal actions against the civilian population," and now this part is important, "and the eventual confirmation of selling the property or statement that the refugees will not return, do not have any legal validity, and are abrogated, null and void ." Now, can one annul anything that happens illegally on the ground by anybody else, by the president -- or, rather, do you agree that this has the force of law, that this order has the force of law?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would hope that it has the force of law. It certainly is a praiseworthy sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I can inform you, with satisfaction, that no document and no act, and there were certain unlawful acts in the municipalities, that none of this was implemented. And may we have 1D427 next, please, on e-court. This is 101, so we don't have to tender that into evidence again. 1D247 next, please. And while we're waiting, let me tell you that the date is the 1st of September, 1992, when your conference was already underway. The number is 247. What did I say? 247. If I misspoke, it's 247. And here in point 2, it says: "All refugee families, regardless of their religion and nationality, are obliged to return to their place of residence in the Serbian Republic in the time and manner stipulated by the plan of returning refugees." Now, this came from the level of the Presidency, with the plan for the refugees' return, and it was sent to Serbia, addressed to Serbia, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, in actual fact, and we did have relations with Serbia, with the ministry. And I would like to remind you that you noticed in your diary that out of a total of, I don't know how many hundreds of thousands of refugees in Serbia, over 15 per cent were Bosnian Serbs who took refuge in Serbia, and that the UN officials -- high-ranking officials informed you that they had been taken in there in a non-discriminatory manner.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Do you remember from your journal that they informed you that our of 320.000 Serbs who had fled from Eastern and Western Bosnia, in addition to that there were 15.000 [as interpreted] Muslims who had fled, and this is a letter stating that they could return in accordance with the plan made for each and every municipality? Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly remember that the refugees -- Muslim refugees were taken, accepted into Serbia, as they were in much greater number into Croatia, and, of course, many of the Muslim refugees went abroad. I mentioned yesterday that a very large number went to Switzerland. One minor point. Dr. Karadzic mentioned that September 1st the -- that on September 1st, the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia was underway. That is not correct. It was opened on September 3rd, the opening day of the International Conference was September 3rd. It's a minor point. I don't mean it as a contentious point. Back to the point of refugees or internally-displaced people. There were, of course, hundreds of thousands, and that was a major issue throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the transcript, could we please correct it? It is 15 per cent, not 15.000. 248, please, could we have that in e-court now. It's the same kind of letter, but it's sent now to the Montenegrin ministry, and it contains the same paragraph number 2. The content is the same. So we wrote the same thing to Montenegro. And could we please have these two documents admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, they will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D247 will be Exhibit D112, and 1D248 will be Exhibit D113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court 249, 1D249. This is a document of the Assembly, not the Presidency, and I'll only deal with paragraph 3 once we have it on our screen: [In English] "All citizens who have left their homes due to war operations, feeling of personal insecurity and jeopardised ... to return to the territory of the Serbian Republic after a durable peace is established. All citizens of other nationalities will be recognised all their rights according to the Constitution and law. "All those who were members of the enemy forces, but have not committed crimes against the Serb people, will not be criminally prosecuted."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, as we can see here, this comes from the level of the Assembly. This is the first pardon for persons who just took part in fighting. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the words say, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have this document admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court inquired yesterday about whether the -- I have only an English version here. I think that's all I was provided, unless there is a technical error. The Court inquired whether the English was -- the original into B/C/S previously. I'd have the same inquiry there. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to ask the same question to the accused. Mr. Karadzic, can you confirm that whether this is the original? The e-court says this is an original document. So whether Bijeljina Assembly issued this declaration in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, this is the Assembly of Republika Srpska. However, they held that session in Bijeljina. So the level is that of the republic, Republika -- so it is the Central Assembly that we're dealing with here. I believe that in the transcript of that session, there is a reference to this document. The OTP has all these transcripts. This document was probably published in both languages. However, you know that our archives were damaged significantly, so we only managed to obtain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With that explanation, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D114, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 65 ter 00041 in e-court. It's a Prosecution number. Page 75 in English, please. In Serbian, it's 77. So could we have page 75 of this document. The Prosecution number is 41. Page 75, we are referring to Vladimir Lukic's expose, who -- he was prime minister at the time. It's the first paragraph here. This isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's line 10, roughly, in the first paragraph: "Already today we must start creating conditions for all citizens who have left their places of residence due to war operations, the feeling of personal insecurity and that of their property, to return to the territory of Republika Srpska, upon establishment of lasting peace. Under the Constitution, we must guarantee the rights of all citizens of other nationalities. We have assumed these obligations, and we must meet them." The prime minister is telling the Assembly here about what the executive is doing in this regard. This is the 19th and 20th of January, 1993. At that point in time, we are together. I think that we were in New York by then, or almost there. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it. That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document that the Prosecution has; all the Assembly transcripts, that is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this paragraph from this document number 41 please be admitted, although it is my understanding that transcripts are being admitted in toto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering 82 pages in English, in its entirety. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D115, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Now I'd like to move on to a different topic, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'd like to move on to another topic. There's quite a bit about this in your journals as well. I would like to ask you whether you remember that all sources of water, except for one small source, and all sources of power in the town of Sarajevo had to come from Serb territory or go via Serb territory. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of the electricity supply to Sarajevo was at issue, and it was resolved peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, they had electricity in Tuzla and Kakanj, and, in a way, we depended on their electricity. However, we controlled the entire water supply. All sources of water were on the Serb side. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask for your journal number 1 to be called up, 06534. Yes, page 36. This is what you wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 784.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you wrote: [In English] "Water supply very difficult. Land convoys are getting through. One got through today." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this section of your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't located it yet, but I'm sure I agree with it. Is it on the left side or the right side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side: "Land convoys above Kumin."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well: "Water supply very difficult. France is providing water supply. Land convoys are getting through." Yes. The issue here clearly was the fact that Sarajevo was under siege by the Bosnian Serb forces, and all supplies had to be admitted through the Bosnian Serb lines. And sometimes they were, and it -- often they were. They had to be negotiated through -- and as I've previously mentioned, the airport had been turned over to UNHCR by the Bosnian Serb forces so that air communication also existed. But on the ground, everything material had to be admitted in through the Bosnian Serb lines, and that was a constant source of discussion. With respect to water that Dr. Karadzic has mentioned, that was difficult, and, indeed -- and, indeed, Western governments and individuals made it possible for the water supply to all parties, all citizens of Sarajevo, be increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. That is correct, to a large extent, because they gave us material for repairs, and we made these repairs possible. Can we see "UNICEF," on the right-hand side: "Water and electricity." [In English] "Muslims control key electric power-plant in Tuzla." [Interpretation] That's also page 36, but it's on the right-hand side. That is what you wrote down; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims remained in control of Tuzla throughout the war. They, of course, were also being shelled, but Tuzla, on the whole, was a pretty safe place to be throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go to page 46 of the same document. 46, "Karadzic," on the left-hand side. Karadzic says: [In English] "We never cut off water and electricity in Sarajevo. We will accept UN people monitoring water and electricity supply. UN people can manage." [Interpretation] In addition to the airport, are we not offering sources of water supply to UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason this conversation took place, and it's reported accurately in the journal, is that the water supply under control of the Bosnian Serbs had been irregular to the point of nonexistent, and it caused a great problem. So this was raised, and here we see that Dr. Karadzic denies having cut off the water supply. You see it in the middle, on the left: "We never cut off the water supply or electricity." That statement was not true, but it was a fact that, after much heavy persuasion, the Bosnian Serbs did agree to allow the water supply of Sarajevo to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will see, Mr. Ambassador, from another document that that is what was done by the other side, for the reasons that we referred to yesterday; to increase the suffering of their own people. So could we have this same document now -- no, actually, 06535, 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P785.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 24, "Karadzic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what you wrote down: [In English] "Not only humanitarian, but also economic. Water and electricity should be under the UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, we were saying all along that the other side resorted to war trickery, with the intention of accusing us. In order to avoid that, we offered that UNPROFOR should be in charge of water and electricity supplies and that corridors should be used for economic supplies, as such, and this led to two UNPROFOR officers saying that Sarajevo was not under blockade, but under a military siege. We'll see that, perhaps, on another day. It's in Mr. Izetbegovic's book. It was not in a blockade, Sarajevo was not. There was an internal blockade. It is smugglers who stopped convoys in order to control rifles and other military equipment, whereas the other side was stopping war supplies in order to tarnish the image of the Serbs, to vilify the Serbs. Do you agree that you wrote that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that a question? That's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Refrain from making comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you write down that we made an offer to the effect that water and electricity should be under UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can read it. It's in front of us. And the reason that we pressed you on that issue was because you had not been permitting regular supplies to go through, and that became an issue and was raised with you. And you agreed, as I note here, that water and electricity could be supplied. This was September 1992. Sarajevo had been under siege since April, five months, so that you could imagine it became an issue, and it was resolved successfully. The siege continued, but the water and electricity were supplied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you have any comment on the statement that the smugglers stopped convoys in order to control rifles and other military equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were smugglers on all sides and all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. One point that I think I mentioned earlier was that criminal elements from all three communities were active throughout the war and made life miserable for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The points made seems to be that it is Bosnians who stopped convoys.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not true. They had the greatest interest in having the convoys come through, since they controlled Sarajevo and Sarajevo was being besieged. I mean, that doesn't make any sense at all and was not true. In addition, UNHCR provided food by air. General McKenzie's book is specific on these points. He was commander of UNPROFOR at this period, a resident in Sarajevo, Canadian General McKenzie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that this was my offer. I said it should be that way. No one asked for it. I wanted to get rid of that burden, and I said it should be UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, these journals have been admitted already, I mean, these numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are admitted in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Thank you. Now I'd like 1D383, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, I would like to remind you, Ambassador, that whenever a humanitarian convoy would pass by, prices went down in Sarajevo. We have proof of that. Prices went down, and the smugglers preferred it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a moment ago, I rose before the Court. I asked the accused to refrain from making comment. I rise again for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. You are just wasting time by making further comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're waiting for the document. That's why I wanted to illuminate a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure we have a translation of this, but I'm going to read it out. It is the Presidency of Republika Srpska -- actually, it is the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Water Management that is writing to us, to the Presidency. They are probably responding to a question that we had put. And the subject is the delivery of water, drinking water, to Sarajevo. The 18th of July, 1993. On that date, at Pale, a meeting was held between the representatives of this ministry and the waterworks companies from the territory of the Serb municipalities of the city of Sarajevo. The agenda of the meeting included the delivery of drinking water to part of Sarajevo that has a predominantly Muslim population, but also with a large number of Serb population that is practically detained in this city. The basic conclusions made at this meeting were as follows: "1. On our side, there is goodwill to deliver the necessary quantities of drinking water. However, in this situation, that is not possible for the following reasons: There is not a continuous flow of electricity to the pumping stations; rather, there are interruptions in the power supply of the pump stations, and that is mostly due to war operations of the Muslim forces. "In the protected areas of water sources, especially in the first and second protection zone of the source of Bacevo, as well as in the general area of this source, there is a large number of personnel and war equipment. New cemeteries are being opened, and dumps are being established. Also, several epidemics have started." Further on: "Some parts of the water supply system is damaged and should be replaced."
