And now could we move on to the second page of this document, please: It says that significant material resources are still lacking for obtaining chemical agents needed for the purification of water. And on the second paragraph, it says: "Along with securing the above-mentioned necessary conditions, the ministry shall, on the basis of the agreed methodology, together with the water supply companies, establish a unit price for the delivery of drinking water in water systems. It should be noted that without proper maintenance of the water supply system, there can be no proper drinking water supplies. We suggest that when there are negotiations with UNPROFOR, expert representatives of the water system should be invited to attend, as was the representatives of this ministry." And at the bottom of the page, we see, written in my own hand, I agree, my signature, "Radovan Karadzic." So the meetings are held with UNPROFOR and with the other side in order to resolve these issues. This was sent to me by the minister, Borivoje Sendic, and I just wrote down "agreed," and I signed my name, "Radovan Karadzic." Do you see this document, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it. I should also note that it was September 1992, that you previously referred to, when you said to Mr. Vance and me that the water supply could be resolved by UNPROFOR. And here it is 10 months later, and it has not yet been resolved. I mention that because it indicates the disparity between words and deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer to say between words and possibilities, because people did receive as much water as was possible. And now here it sets out how this could be supplied in a continuous fashion, so the accent there is on continuous supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, and we will supply a translation of it in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D116, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the next document is 1D895 that I'd like called up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the document, Mr. Ambassador, let me ask you this: Do you know Morton Abramowitz?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I spoke to him on the phone several times, I never met him personally, but do you know his friend, Fred Cuny?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Fred died in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was there at the behest of the well-known financier and philanthropist George Soros. The reason he was there was precisely this very question, the water supply of Sarajevo, because of the Bosnian Serb siege of the city: And Abramowitz at this time was working closely with Soros in an effort to resolve the problem, and they sent Cuny there, who helped quite a lot until he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. And Morton Abramowitz, otherwise, was a high-ranking official; right? I think he was in the Council for Foreign Policy, or whatever, but at any rate, he was a prominent individual. Now, on this document -- in this document --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Retired diplomat. He was a retired Foreign Service officer. He had been ambassador to Turkey and was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a long letter from Fred Cuny to Morton Abramowitz, and it's dated -- we'll find the date. Let's see when he's writing this to Morton Abramowitz. Anyway, we found this letter over the internet. May we have page 6 of this document displayed, please. Yes, the date is January 1994. Page 6, please. Paragraph 1, page 6: [In English] "One of the officers in the UNPROFOR claims that they have information that some members of government are opposed to turning on the water because it will take away one of the most omnipresent images of suffering in the city. According to this source, the radicals in the government feel they need to offset the negative publicity that the Bosnians have been getting due to their siege of Vitez by -- with images of Sarajevans carrying water, fuel," and so on, "under the Serbs' shelling. (I personally discount this theory given all the publicity the system has received, but UNPROFOR thinks it's a possibility.)" [Interpretation] So I think we can believe this man, Cuny, can't we?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the writer of the letter does not believe him, because he says: "I personally discount this theory ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now, on page 5 -- well, he's receiving information from UNPROFOR, and UNPROFOR is present in the field more than he is, and is trying to inform objectively, but says that information is coming in about that from UNPROFOR. Page 5, please: [In English] "We have been told by someone close to Dr. Mohammed Zlatar that the reason that some officials are trying to prevent the water from being turned on is that the officials are engaged in selling water from the brewery and Bacevo. Tankers routinely take water from those sources and deliver it to a number of enterprises, including the Holiday Inn. Some is also sold to households. Water sales are brisk, especially during the winter. Our information tells us that the city will eventually allow us to turn on the water, but only after they have limited the area served (by closing critical valves) and after the winter, when the demand and price for water deliveries will drop - thus, the three-month testing regime." [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, I was astonished to learn of this and reports about this that I got from our own people, not from the United Nations. Now, do you see that they were selling water and that our assistance in water supplies upset their prices?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already established that there was criminal activity by all sides, Dr. Karadzic, and this item, which I see now for the first time, confirms that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 6 -- or that was page 6. Staying with page 6, paragraph 3: [In English] "If the government continues to stonewall us, we have several options. I could ask General Rose to simply order us to turn on the system or turn it over to the UN. That may be the easiest and politically the best way for the Bosnians to deal with that." [Interpretation] It's a long letter, but in this letter Mr. Cuny claims that we enabled water maintenance to be carried out and that they informed the Muslims that the water should be allowed to run, but that the Muslim government did not accept the water being switched on, and that the authority switched it on regardless of that, and that they came and shut the water supply off to prevent it from reaching the city of Sarajevo. That's what the gist of this letter is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more complicated than that, Dr. Karadzic. If one looks at the very next paragraph, it reads, I quote: "I would like to mention that we have a lot of support from various sectors of the government." No surprise there. We had a divided government, as we've discussed frequently, about the Bosnian government divided as between secularists and religious people, divided between military and civilian, divided between those who sought to appease the attacking Serbs, and those who sought to accommodate them. There were divisions within the government. I don't think there's any argument about that. There were divisions within most governments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, may we have page 2 displayed, please, paragraph 1 -- the middle of paragraph 1 on page 2, please: [In English] "However, after --" [Interpretation] Paragraph 1, the top of the page: [In English] "However, we have been unable to persuade the city authorities to allow us to turn it on, even during the heavy shelling that occurred in January. At one point, after several people were killed trying to collect water from the taps at the brewery, I ordered the water turned on on my own authority, but the authorities intervened and cut it off."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, not the Serb authorities, the Muslim authorities, they didn't allow the water to be turned on and flow into the city. Is that the conclusion that one can draw from this letter? And I'm not interested in factions of the government, but the government, as a whole, that succeeded against his order to turn the water supply off again for the town to suffer?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the conclusion we could draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender 1D895 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D117.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have on e-court 1D336, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'm not sure that we have the translation of that, but this was obtained from the Prosecution. It's the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the Muslim part, the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces, the Security Administration, copy number 1, dated the 23rd of October, 1993. On page 2 -- may we have page 2, please. It reads: "The president of the Novi Grad municipality, Enes Cengic, in talks with the narrow portion of the Command of the 101st Motorised Brigade, presented a number of security-related information about the functioning and problems of civilian authority in this municipality. He stressed the -- Ismet Hadzic, the commander of the 5th Motorised Brigade --" he made particular reference to Ismet Hadzic, Huso Cesir [phoen], Ismet's assistant for logistics, and Sefkija Okeric, the former president of the Executive Board of the municipality, who are hard-line advocates of the SDA policy and intend to raise the Muslim people about -- against the legally-elected organs of Novi Grad municipality." We don't have to read this further, but it says lower down otherwise: "Cengic stresses that the citizens and fighters of Dobrinja do not support the conduct and work of the Command of the 5th Motorised Brigade, which they demonstrated through a petition for which they collected 500 signatures, asking that the commander and Command of the 5th Motorised Brigade be replaced, as well as the Command of the Civilian Protection." In the petition which Cengic had on him or with him, the petition stresses irregularities with respect to humanitarian aid and assistance, because individuals are being deprived the right of that assistance and aid, and that the stream is focused on the priorities -- on giving priority to the commander and his friends? Now, this is a secret police intelligence report, or, rather, the military intelligence report, to the effect that their commander, which uses the electricity that he received through Serb territory instead of giving the electricity to hospitals and other needy institutions, he is connecting them up to his friends' flats and homes. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you mentioned this is October 1993. I ceased my direct activity with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina in May 1993, so I was not aware of this since I had nothing officially to do with Bosnia in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't deny that or challenge it, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you produced it and I read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender 1D366 into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the accused indicated, Your Honour, there is no translation, we haven't had a chance to see it, so that will need to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be marked for identification as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D118, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have displayed now on -- do they have it on e-court? Yes. 1D899 next, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, while we're waiting for that to come up, I would like to tell you what it's about. It's the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, and it is an appeal to the Muslims to cease their hostilities. And it is dated May 1992. 1D899 is the number. May we have the English version displayed on our screens, and I'll read it out in Serbian. So may we have the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have 1D899.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's entitled: "Announcement to Muslims, appeal for cessation of hostilities." "To all Muslim men and women, the unfortunate fragmentation of Yugoslavia and the anti-constitutional secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, as well as the tyrannist policy of the Croat-Muslim coalition, have shoved us into the worst of civil wars, religious and ethnic war. The fragmentation of Yugoslavia also led to the transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three units. A number of Muslims and Croats is to live in the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, a number of Serbs is to live in the Muslim and Croat Bosnia and Herzegovina. It may be you who will live in the Muslim or the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. That will depend on political agreement, which is inevitable. For the time being, you are in Serb BH, and you are to enjoy the same rights as the Serbs do. Many Muslim villages have laid down their arms and are enjoying the full protection of the Serb Army and Serb state organs. Since we are dealing with a religious war, we do not bind them to fight on our side. And in all other respects, they are equal with the Serbs. The Muslims are being treated in our hospitals, which are also their hospitals. Muslim women are giving birth successfully in the Sokolac Hospital. Food is provided both by Serbs and by Muslims who are not fighting against the Serbs. "Why are you waging war against the Serbs? Can't we preserve peace and wait for a political solution? Why should your families starve? Why should you live in forests, where you may fear winter? How many Serbs and Muslims are to be killed for the crazy ideas of an Islamic state?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question? What's the point of reading out your statement at the time? Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, can one see, on the basis of what has been read out so far, that the Serb side is not counting on a fait accompli and [indiscernible]; rather, they believe that ultimately there will be a political solution as to which part of Bosnia will belong to who?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find this document thoroughly disingenuous, Dr. Karadzic. I must tell you that frankly. The statement at the end, for example, I quote: "The West will not allow it, for the West wants you Muslims to be obliterated in battle with the Serbs and the Croats." No statement could be more ridiculous than that. In addition, it has to be remembered that this was May 1992. You said that yourself. And it was on May 12 that the Bosnian Serb Assembly issued that directive or statement, I'm not quite sure what you called it, the one that gave your war aims. It's been introduced into the court. We discussed it extensively in the Krajisnik case. And it was clear, from your official document, what and where you wanted the borders of your self-declared Republika Srpska to be. That's what it was largely about. And those borders would have given you about, roughly, two-thirds to 75 per cent of the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's one of the major issues that the war was all about. And so I find this appeal to be consistent with your policy, with the policy of the Bosnian Serbs, in the sense that it called for the Muslims basically to surrender, since you were doing very well on the ground. No surprise there. We've established that. But as for the reasoning behind it, it is untrue to the point of ridiculousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, I will tell you a few things now that I will prove here while you're here and later. There is widespread belief among some Serb and Muslim intellectuals that the West had intended to neutralise the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina by using the Serbs and Croats. Are you denying that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger, I take it that he is putting his case to the witness. Thank you. Yes, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's nonsense. The sympathy of the West, whether correct or incorrect, was overwhelmingly on the side of the Muslims. We've established that already. Dr. Karadzic has made that point repeatedly, and it's correct. That's why, for example, somebody like Fred Cuny had been sent by George Soros to Sarajevo to see what could be done with the water supply. That's why UNPROFOR was there, that's why all of this happened. So to say that the West intended to neutralise the Muslims in Bosnia by using the Serbs and Croats is not only beyond belief, it's laughable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now I will have to add even more evidence coming from Muslim sources. However, I would like to ask you whether you were part of that international community that was overwhelmingly on the side of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I was a negotiator for and with the United Nations. You know that, Dr. Karadzic, as well as I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that your journals are impartial, but not your testimony. That will compel me to introduce yet another topic that I had intended to spare us of. We have Izetbegovic's book, where he says that President Tudjman told him that the European Community had entrusted him with taking care of the Bosnian Muslims, and Izetbegovic was opposed to that. Are you saying that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not present when this statement that you say President Tudjman made to President Izetbegovic. I rather doubt it, unless what he means to be saying is that the words "to take care of the Bosnian Muslims," meant that he should support them, meant that he should be with them in their struggle against you. I regard that statement as just rather ambiguous, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read out what Izetbegovic had written: "As for Tudjman's bragging that some Europeans had entrusted to him the Europisation of the Bosnian Muslims and the prevention of the creation of a Muslim state on European soil, I think that there was some truth in these stories of Tudjman's. Many in Europe and America, with a few honourable exceptions, viewed with suspicion what was going on in Bosnia. What they considered to be Islamic revival in the country needed to be extinguished. Many ugly things were done in order to achieve this. One of them was the criminalisation of the Bosnian authorities in the BH that would intensify after the war and culminate in a 'New York Times' article in 1999." I assure you, Mr. Ambassador, that an MP of ours also said -- I mean, we were chosen to be the executors of the Muslims, and we refused to be that. Executioners, rather. The thesis among the Muslim intellectuals is that it is the West that gets the biggest possible advantage from a conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims. Regardless of whether this is true or not, that is deeply rooted. We will find it in Izetbegovic's books, in Zulfikarpasic's books. Are you denying that, as you did a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to Tudjman's bragging, that is, what Izetbegovic called Tudjman's bragging, that's believable, because as we know, as I've testified, it's been made very clear from my journals, Tudjman had great disrespect and dislike for Muslims. He routinely referred to me, when discussing Izetbegovic, as "that fundamentalist Izetbegovic," and this is well known. There is no argument about that. There's also no argument about the Bosnian Serb and Serbian interest, along with the Bosnian Croat and Croatian interest, in dividing -- in carving up Bosnia and partitioning it. That's been well established. What is odd and unbelievable in what you've read is that it suddenly makes the Muslims the guilty party, on the part of the West. You spent the last three days, Dr. Karadzic, in seeking to make the point that the Bosnian Serbs were incorrectly opposed by the West, and now you're coming forth with this document that claims, quite incorrectly, that the West, whatever that means, are suddenly wanting to see the Bosnian Muslims wiped out. I can assure you, Dr. Karadzic, that Bosnia-Herzegovina -- not one person in 10.000 in America had heard of Bosnia-Herzegovina before 1992, and the points in this document that you're reading, somehow that Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied some special place in Western policy, whatever that was supposed to be, is entirely fanciful. There's no -- there's nothing to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, like everywhere else in the world, the broad masses who do not know about Bosnia-Herzegovina do not actually pursue policy. It is governments that pursue policy. And the Western governments knew full well everything about the Balkans. However, a small correction, Mr. Ambassador. Izetbegovic is not saying that all of this is bragging. He says, I think that there was some truth in these stories of Tudjman's. Another correction, Mr. Ambassador. The Serbs besieged the Bosnian Muslims to have Bosnia remain as a whole, together with them, in Yugoslavia, not to have any kind of partition. Partition was advocated by Alija Izetbegovic, as we will prove here.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, let me remind you of your statement to us, which is in my diary, that the problem could be solved if Tudjman and Mate Boban, the Bosnian Croat leader, were on one side of the table and you, Milosevic, and Hadzic were on the other side of the table. What that meant -- and you can comment on this, of course. What that meant to everybody who read that statement, meant that the Serbs and the Croats were interested in the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the legal fiction of maintaining a state called "Bosnia-Herzegovina," in which, in effect and in reality, the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Had you been told that after the crisis in Croatia had been resolved, or, rather, the question of the Serb Krajina in Croatia, you would have been right. However, my thesis was always that it was Serb-Croat relations that lay at the heart of the Yugoslav crises, and that we could not make any progress in Bosnia because the question of the Serb Krajina had not been resolved. That was the point. That is why we needed Tudjman and Milosevic, not for Bosnia, because if the question of the Serb Krajina were to be resolved, then it would be easier to find a solution for Bosnia. I will remind you, Mr. Ambassador, that up until the breakout of the war, throughout 1991 we were making offers to Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia, and we were giving up on all regionalisations. That is the agreement reached between us and the Muslim Bosniak organisation. At first, it was supported by Izetbegovic, but after that, these chances went down the drain. Are you denying that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct when you say that the principal issue in the conflict, the principal underlying issue, was always the relationship between Serbia and Croatia. They are the two largest republics in the former Yugoslavia, and the relationship between Zagreb and Belgrade was essential. It still is. Where you are incorrect, Dr. Karadzic, is when you say that, Throughout 1991, we were making offers to Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia. Why you were making those offers is clear. The reason you were making those offers is that Yugoslavia was breaking up, and with the departure of Croatia and Slovenia, the two richest and wealthiest republics in the old Yugoslavia, with their departure the rump Yugoslavia became, in effect, a Serbian state, because it would consist of Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro, and neither the Croats nor the Muslims wanted to remain in a Serbo-Slavia. That's what they used to call it. They told that to us frequently, there's no more Yugoslavia, it's a Serbo-Slavia. And that's why they didn't want to remain in Yugoslavia, and that is why in the vote independence on February 29 and March 1, 1992, the vote that your party boycotted, they voted in favour of independence. That point has been established. In my opinion, that point has been established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll get back to that. Excellency, D899, can we have that admitted now? It's still available to us, and we will see which villages -- which Muslim villages lived in peace in our parts up until the end of the war, so we will see how sincere he was. As for this page 252 of Izetbegovic's book, perhaps we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, first 1D899.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're starting a bit from scratch on that, Your Honour. I don't think that was notified to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can anticipate a particular problem, but I think prudence requires me to at least review it and give it the consideration I would have had it been notified earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be an excerpt -- a compilation of his speeches, so shall we mark it for identification for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution does have six volumes of my speeches, orders, et cetera, and this is on page 233 of Volume 4, I think. Yes, book number 4. That was published while I was in hiding. It was published by the Committee for the Truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for President Izetbegovic's book, what number is it, in terms of 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, as the ambassador's testimony developed, I was compelled to draw on this argument which I did have in mind, but I did not offer it because I didn't want to deal with this particular topic with this witness. This stemmed from Ambassador Okun's allegations that this appeal of mine was disingenuous. We are discussing whether the West pursued a perfidious policy against the Serbs and Muslims, and there are many books that state that in the West as well. Many Muslims think that that was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the relevant passage was read into the transcript. We don't need to admit it separately, so we'll not deal with that book right now. I see the time. It's time to have a second break. And given that you have had almost 12 hours with the ambassador, I think you should be able to finish your cross-examination in three-quarters of an hour when we resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a brief statement in connection with what Dr. Karadzic just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Karadzic, I'm surprised to hear you say that I alleged that your appeals were disingenuous. I said the opposite. I said they were praiseworthy, I said they were commendable, I said they had merit. I said they were not observed in the field, but I never accused those documents of being anything but sincere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I believe that you know of a psychology test that is called "Unfinished Sentences" in our language. May I remind you, that's a test in which the client is given an unfinished sentence, and then everyone finishes the sentence whichever way they wish or feel. At any rate, there are no two identical finishing parts of a sentence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that in your journals, and I consider them to be invaluable material, a lot was written on the basis of these unfinished sentences. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what you mean by that, Dr. Karadzic, because the journals record what people said. Occasionally, in fact often a bit more than occasionally, I would note my own comments on what they were saying at the time, whether I believed them, or disbelieved them, or that sort of thing, in order to make it possible for me, in retrospect, to understand what they were saying. But I don't think that the concept of unfinished sentences really applies. I think in negotiations there are always positions taken that are sometimes worthy, sometimes unworthy, sometimes are put out just to test the waters, so to speak; but I'm not sure that I could call these unfinished sentences. Excuse me, but that's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I meant was that the readers of your journals would engage in that. However, there is no doubt about one thing. Your journals were in statu nascendi, they were created at the time when the phenomena actually took place, when talks were held, et cetera; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And your point -- the earlier point you make, that the readers of the note-books could draw different conclusions from them, is also correct. But I should mention that they were not a momentary product. They began in October 1991 and stretch into May 1993, so they covered a good period of time and allowed me to make better and better judgements as time went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope that all the participants -- actually, I'd like to have something distributed. What I like about your entire testimony is the part that pertains to the journals. Perhaps I'm a bit surprised by the part that came after the "but" that you would insert, and that would actually be expert testimony, expert opinion. I wouldn't mind, because who would do it better? However, then I'd have to have different preparations. I made an analysis here, or, rather, my team did, as to how your subsequent testimony -- or, rather, to what extent is it based on what is written in the journals, so I would like us to go through that quickly, if you agree. So the first part, we called it "Okun versus Okun." I hope you don't mind. So let us have a look at this. The most important topic is that of ethnic cleansing. So the first and second assertion -- that's what you said, actually, when you testified in Mr. Krajisnik's trial on the 22nd of June, 2004. You can see which pages, 41 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is read out too fast and we do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you said during your testimony is something that we did not find at all in your journal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What are you referring to, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said, "Excuse me," Ambassador, just wait a minute. Since the interpreters were not provided with this document, they have difficulty following you, given that you are reading out so fast, and then they stopped interpreting your statement after you made: "When you testified in Mr. Krajisnik's trial on the 22nd of June ..." And then please continue from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ambassador, number 1 and number 2, the assertions made here, that is what you said on the 22nd of June, 2004, on page 4158 and 4204. And the second assertion also in the Krajisnik trial on the 22nd of June, 2004, on page 4169, and this is the assertion: [In English] "Bosnian Serbs had six political goals. Third, to be ethnically pure Serb or overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "At a later stage, the Bosnian Serbs were removing Muslims from their territories to create an ethnically-pure Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] We're going to prove very easily that that wasn't the case, but the Defence and I personally would like you to go away from that conviction too, that that was not so. Why is that not contained in the diaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points, Dr. Karadzic. It is contained in the diaries. It is perfectly clear from the diaries [Realtime transcript read in error "It's clear on the points]. The second point, on the question of ethnically pure, that was the term used by Mr. Krajisnik, himself, when he gave that video representation of the Republika Srpska in which he claimed and stated that the Republika Srpska occupied land that was Serb before the war, and that was demonstrably untrue because the very map he was using indicated all the Muslim opstina along the Drina. Last, but not least, the statement about the war aims, the goals of the Bosnian Serbs, I stated were known publicly and privately, and that is true, because on May 12, 1992, as we've discussed previously, your government issued those war aims, and they were fully consistent with the six that I have listed in previous trials. And in the Milosevic case, he agreed with me that those were the Bosnian Serb war aims, if you read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador, if you could take a look at the transcript, the starting point of your answer doesn't seem to correctly reflect what you said in the first point. It just said: "It's clear on the points --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember you having said that it's clear from the journal, itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What I said was I was drawing a correct conclusion from my note-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't find that in your note-books, neither did my team find it either. Now, I'd like to clear up two or three other points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, linguistic problems in this Tribunal are considerable because of the idioms used, and I'm going to rely on the fact that the interpreters confirm that according to an idiom in our language, when it says that it's purely Serb territory, it means incontestably Serbian, that is, over 50 per cent Serbs. Now, in my testimony in the Krajisnik trial, I underlined that. If we say that something is purely Croatian or Muslim, it doesn't mean that it has been cleansed of the rest, but that it is, without a doubt, incontestably that. So we recognised 80 per cent of territory being incontestably Serbian, Muslim, or Croatian, and that 20 per cent had to be resolved in some other way. Now, this specific feature of our language might have led to this misunderstanding. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have, but it didn't. Let me recall for you your own statement in January 1993 to the combined Serbian -- Bosnian Serb Co-ordinating Committee, in which you describe the situation in Zvornik 50:50 per cent Serbian and Muslim before the war, and now the same population, 50.000, you said -- actually, it was bigger than 50.000, but you said 50.000, now 100 per cent Serb. So I certainly accept your linguistic -- your semantic differentiation of the word "purely," which can also, in English, mean "incontestably," but it also was used to describe the ethnic cleansing as it was taking place. Indeed, you, yourself, described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to go back to the January 1993 meeting, I have to say this: Prior to that sentence of mine, Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic advocated to have the exclusion -- advocated against the forcible removal of any of the population, and I supported him, and I said that, Why would we do that, because it's happening spontaneously? So I didn't justify it, I didn't advocate the displacement of the population. I just said, What would forcible displacement mean if the population was moving of its own accord? That's all I wanted to say. Now, I'd like us to go back to this analysis, an analysis of --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I comment on that? I'll be brief. Jovanovic was the foreign minister of first Yugoslavia and then Serbia, and at the relevant meeting that Dr. Karadzic and I are discussing, the meeting of June -- of January 1993 of the Co-ordinating Committee, he began his remarks by saying that he was no expert. Jovanovic said that he was no expert on the specific situation of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but, as an experienced diplomat, he knew of the exchanges of populations peacefully that occurred after the First World War as between Greece and Turkey, and that's a well-known fact, and he was suggesting to the group, the Serb Co-ordinating Committee - I guess he was actually suggesting it primarily to the Bosnian Serbs - that that was a way to accomplish their goal, that they didn't have to forcibly expel people, that they could do it peacefully. That was his remark. That's a matter of record. You can read it in the Co-ordinating Committee document which was entered into the Krajisnik trial. And I should say Krajisnik never contested that point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may we have the six strategic goals? It's 00781, a Prosecution document, or, rather, it's an exhibit already. And I'd like to point out there, as I did during the Krajisnik testimony, that the third goal was that the Drina should not be the border between two worlds, meaning there the East and the West, because that's what the Drina River was, not between the Serbs, as it stated in the Krajisnik trial, but between two worlds, and that is quite clear in the original. And nowhere in those goals does it state that the Serb unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be ethnically pure or overwhelmingly Serbian. Now, can we have the document with those goals put up on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're right on one count, Mr. Ambassador. It was no secret, and already in June we had decided that, together with the map, we send the European Community those goals as our starting point for the negotiations. Of course, we had to count on losing something, some of that, forfeiting some of that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've mentioned, Dr. Karadzic, previously, and I don't want to take your time or the Court's time, that your goals published on May 12th, 1992, were largely geographic in nature; that if one had put them into reality, that horseshoe around Sarajevo we've discussed previously would have been fully affected. You, for example, wanted your western border, that is, the border on the eastern side of the horseshoe in the Neretva Valley, and you made that claim for quite a long period. The Croats, of course, denied it and then defeated you in a battle there. They were not about to let you get the Neretva, since their self-declared capital, Mostar, is on the Neretva. So these issues stayed in contention during the war, but I cannot agree with you when you say that your goals, as stated in May, were inconsistent with the goals that I have described. I think they were fully consistent, so I disagree with you on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well, Mr. Ambassador. It doesn't say that we're calling for an ethnically-pure state anywhere. That's what this is about. And I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber that the transcription -- the transcribing of those goals is termed a decision one year later due to some personnel replacement in the administration. So could I have it on the record that in my speech at the Assembly, in the transcript that we have here it says that the Drina should not be the border between worlds or two worlds, and that is in keeping with what Mr. Izetbegovic said, that Una will not be a border for the Croats and the Drina a border for the Serbs, and that it will be open, but that I said that they will be -- I termed them "soft borders," as certain borders in Europe are. Now, Mr. Ambassador, if we look at number 3, you said: [In English] "Karadzic said we want peace or it would be disastrous." [Interpretation] Now, in your testimony, and that is to be found -- that third statement is to be found in your note-book number 4, 06530, page 46 -- at page 46, but in relation to this you testified in the Krajisnik trial, on the 22nd of June, 2004, on page 4400, there was an addition, and it says: [In English] "Okun does not believe he was being sincere when he said that unless he meant that it would be disastrous for Muslims and Croats." [Interpretation] Do you agree, Mr. Ambassador, that the Serbs were a third of the population, and the anti-Serb coalition amounted to two-thirds, and that it was Croatia, with five million inhabitants, temporarily or permanently was against them, that is, in the ratio of 1:8, and with the inclusion of the West against the Serbs in Bosnia the ratio was 1 to an indefinable number? So why did we want war? Why did you add this in your testimony, whereas it does not exist in your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's easy to answer, Mr. Karadzic. I'll be brief. It's important not to take each entry -- each statement of yours in isolation. You said war would be disastrous. I was well aware that before that, in October 1991, when you walked out of the old Bosnian Assembly, you said if they declared independence, that would lead the Muslims on a path to hell, so that I was taking your remarks in the total context, not in the individual case. Now, when you say that you were heavily outnumbered, you have failed to mention that you had behind you Serbia, with 10 million people, and the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, with almost half a million troops. So your contention that you were the weaker party, particularly at the beginning, is clearly not the case, since the JNA was totally with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to enter into a debate there. Mr. Ambassador, do you remember that Serbia accepted any plan and all plans, and that this co-ordinating body was established at the proposal of the West, saying that Serbia could keep us under control and influence us, and that our first disagreements with Serbia came with the Vance-Owen Plan which Serbia accepted, but we didn't; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan, after it was accepted by the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, it was not accepted by the Bosnian Serbs, the only party not to accept it. And the Serbs, led personally by President Milosevic, in my presence, made what I regarded as a sincere effort to convince Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik to accept the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. They never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Please believe me that they were more than sincere, and that's where we and the Serbian leadership disagreed completely. Now, I'm interested in why there are so many differences here. And looking at point 4 there, you say, in the transcript of the Krajisnik trial on the 22nd of June, 2004, page 4172: [In English] "Tie Serb opstinas to Yugoslavia. Otherwise, war will result."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was you who said that, Dr. Krajisnik -- excuse me, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why isn't that in your diary, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is in the diary. Can we check it? I would be happy to do so, but it might take too much time. But I would suggest that the Court, the Defence, and the counsel check it, because I think it's in the note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Ambassador, of our priorities. The first priority was that the whole Yugoslavia should remain with six republics. The second priority was Bosnia and anybody else who wanted to. The third priority, which Izetbegovic proposed, was that only the Muslim parts of Bosnia step down from Yugoslavia, and we'll prove that quite easily here and demonstrate it. It's contained in Muslim sources. And in that case, then, it would be the type according to West Virginia, the Serb variant that Serb opstinas remain within Yugoslavia. The fourth priority was that these municipalities, too, should step down from Yugoslavia, but be given their unit. So I think it's all this case of unfinished sentences once again.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can understand you would say that, Dr. Karadzic, and it's partially true. That is to say, your priorities were to, in the first case, make no change in the Yugoslav administrative structure. But, of course, there was change that already happened. Croatia had declared independence and pretty much gained it. Slovenia had declared it and completely gained its independence. And the situation that you mention of West Virginia, which we've discussed previously, differs in this case: You made and make the point that West Virginia seceded from Virginia while the Civil War was in progress because they were not a slave-holding area, and that is correct. The difference between the West Virginia case and your case is that you effectively started the war in Bosnia with your self-declared declaration that you would either remain in Yugoslavia or have your own Republika Srpska. So while the West Virginia case was the result of a war, your declaration started the war. I do not expect you to agree with that, but it is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have proof and evidence, Mr. Ambassador, that the unilateral -- and all your colleagues from the West, from Warren Christopher, even President Clinton, James Bissett, and so on, Henry Kissinger, all of them say quite the reverse, the unilateral secession. And even in the Milosevic judgement, it says Slovenia proclaimed independence and caused the war. Now, later on, they amend that, but even this OTP says that the fact that Slovenia had stepped down caused the war. And I say that the unconstitutional proclamation of independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina caused the war, not us. We didn't need a war. We didn't -- weren't seeking to acquire their territories. But let's move on. That's something that we shall prove and show here quite easily. But all I want to tell you is that there are enormous differences between the note-books, which I accept, and your testimony, in your subsequent testimony, that is to say, 10 years later. There are quite a lot of examples of that. For example, if we look at point 13 on page 2, you testified to the fact that Milosevic -- you said that the Greek president, although Milosevic was on good terms with the prime minister, not the president -- anyway, you say Milosevic would accept 45 per cent of B and H land for Bosnian Serbs: [In English] "But it's hard to accept the segment given to the Bosnian Serbs by the Vance-Owen Plan, because it is not ethnically clean. So the negotiators had a problem, because they cannot support ethnic cleansing by Milosevic is saying he will accept 45 per cent if it is ethnically clean. The leadership of Republika Srpska was even tougher." [Interpretation] There's none of that in the diaries, Mr. Ambassador, and our objection/comment was not ethnic purity, but poverty, because we got 10 or 15 per cent of the common wealth. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Dr. Karadzic. You will find in my journals numerous comments particularly by Aleksa Buha, your colleague, in effect the foreign minister of the so-called Republika Srpska. You'll find in the note-books numerous comments by Buha that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was unfair to the Bosnian Serbs, among other reasons, because it did not put them all together. His specific charge was that 50 per cent of the Bosnian Serbs were not in Bosnian Serb majority provinces. The fact is it was about 40 per cent. But he was correct, because the very purpose of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was to cure the ethnic cleansing, was to end it, and mix the parties so they could live in a postwar peaceful Bosnia-Herzegovina all together, the way they had before the war. So, Dr. Karadzic, this superb exercise you've gone through in parsing my journals, and I appreciate that you have found them effective, but you have and your team has been very selective in what you've chosen, and, therefore, in many respects it is misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ambassador, here's what you wrote with respect to Mitsotakis, and it's journal number 2, 0635 is the number. The page number is 53: [In English] "Mitsotakis: We must solve Serb-Croat differences. They are ready to talk. Today, Muslims are the problem." [Interpretation] And that's what you wrote about Mitsotakis. Now, in your testimony, you say that the comments made by the Serbs is that the territories they receive were not ethnically pure, they were poor territories, no infrastructure, no industry, no mines. And we have a whole study conducted why the Vance-Owen Plan is unacceptable, was unacceptable. A whole study was conducted, and I'm going to present it to this Trial Chamber. It was a contemporaneous study, where it says how much of the housing fund was given to the Serbs, how many mines and mineral ores and so on, and these were territories which had been Serb for centuries. So is this not a drastic difference between the diary and the testimony?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the least, Dr. Karadzic. I have pointed that out. I just again pointed out what Buha said, and Buha used to make that point to us -- to me regularly. He would say, in his colourful terminology, The only thing you've given us are the snakes and the stones. So there was no secret there. Also, it should be noted that the Prime Minister Mitsotakis of Greece was a very strong supporter of the Serbian position throughout the war, both Serb and Bosnian Serb position. Indeed, it was he who convened the conference in Athens when you signed, under heavy pressure, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan on May 2nd, 1993. And as you and I know, he went to the Bosnian Serb Assembly with President Milosevic a couple of weeks later in May to try to convince you to sign again and to agree to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and you rejected his plea and you rejected Milosevic's plea, and the war continued for two more years, until the Croatians ended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you this: Did you understand Mr. Buha correctly? What language was he speaking to you, what language did he say that in?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke to us in both English and Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that his English is not good even today, and it was even worse at the time. But "stones and snakes," so it wasn't a question of the population; it was a question of poverty. And this confirms that our objections were because of the natural resources and the infrastructure, which the plan provided for, didn't it? Now, we have your Athens notes here on the screen, on e-court, the Athens notes, entries. Can you find anywhere among them, Mr. Ambassador -- can you find this: [In English] "The Serbs are ready to accept less than 50 per cent. Milosevic would help." [Interpretation] So this relates to the Bosnian Serbs, that they're ready to accept less than 50 per cent, although we always counted 30 per cent for the Muslims, 70 per cent to the Croats, and 53 per cent to the Serb -- now, this entry, can it lead to this kind of testimony?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has never been any dispute between us and I have never said that you insisted on holding all of the land that your army occupied. I have stated, and it is correct, that the army -- the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS, occupied about 70 per cent of the territory, but it was clear at all times that there would have to be some adjustment to this. Now, in the Vance-Owen Plan, you ended up with 43 per cent of the territory, that is to say, 43 per cent in Serb-majority provinces. That would have required your forces to withdraw from about 40 per cent of the land they occupied at the time. Vance and Owen thought that was fair. They were heavily criticised in certain quarters in the West, above all in the United States, for, quote, "legitimatising" ethnic cleansing and, quote, "legitimatising" Serb aggression. They did not agree with that at all, because they felt that reducing your occupation from 70 per cent to 43 per cent was something of an achievement. But that was the reality, that they were attacked for it. And as we know, the Bosnian Serbs were not the only party that rejected the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. The US government rejected it. That you were willing to accept less than your army occupied was never a point at issue, since the army had been very successful in taking three-quarters of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, conclude your cross-examination in 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Ambassador, that at the Carrington-Cutileiro conference, without a war and before the war, we agreed to even less than we had gotten now, 45 per cent, and without contiguous territories, when it was assumed that Bosnia would not go into war? That was even less than were we got now; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We saw that on the Darwin draft map. I agree it was in the draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I'm running short of time, I would now like to draw your attention to part 4. Since we cannot go through all of it, I would like to say, though, that the analysis shows significant discrepancies in relation to the diary that I highly appreciate. Look at paragraph 2: [In English] "Karadzic says that Trnopolje was an open camp where people were free to come and go, but that is not true. When asked about phasing out the camp, Karadzic forecast on Serbs being held by others, which is true, but they were held in much smaller numbers." [Interpretation] That is a transcript of your testimony in Krajisnik the same day, the same year. The page is 4200 and 4201. Now let us see -- well, Ambassador, there is no reference to that in your diaries. Trnopolje was always an open camp, and there were more Serbs in prisons, except for these prisoners of war who were released very soon. I'm afraid that something happened between the period when you kept your diary and the period when you testified. What can you say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that's not true, Dr. Karadzic, except that, of course, with the passage of time we all learn things. I refer to you again Cornelius Sommaruga's speech of August 26, 1992, at the London Conference, in which he listed the detention centres, the bad ones, the ones where people were horribly mistreated, and they were all detention centres run by the Bosnian Serbs. He also, and this is in the record, used the number several hundred thousand. He also gave as an example - I have not mentioned this previously, but it's in Dr. Sommaruga's speech - that at Sanski Most, the Bosnian Serbs -- he doesn't say it specifically, but Sanski Most had been taken by the Bosnian Serbs, so it's clearly the Bosnian Serbs he's referring to. At Sanski Most, civilians were driven across the battle-field between the lines. I find it very hard, Dr. Karadzic, agree with you, although it is flattering that you've paid such attention to my journals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a unique opportunity, Mr. Ambassador, that we have a person like yourself here. What I wish to say is you've just confirmed that that is based on your subsequent knowledge. I'm afraid that Mr. Sommaruga was also misinformed, or, rather, incompletely and incorrectly informed. I would like to draw your attention to page 2, paragraph 3, where it says: [In English] "Karadzic: Wants political settlement of our situation. We have to arrive at a solution. Cannot abandon sovereignty and equality of our people or our land. We'll shortly close last prisoner of war camps, give war criminals over to the ICRC. No offensives from us. Unilateral cease-fire already declared. Ready to talk until a solution is found, but cannot accept: 1, unitary state; 2, central state; 3, loss of national status or our land." [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, that is in your diary. I can confirm it now as well. It is Volume 6, note-book number 6, 06539, page 9. So you very faithfully recorded what my position was: No unitary state, no centralised state, and we cannot lose our status of nation and become a national minority. However, your testimony is different. That's why I'm afraid that someone misinformed you later on. While you were in a position to see things for yourself on the spot, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what your question is, Dr. Karadzic, but let me respond as I understand it. I recorded correctly, and I'm pleased to hear you agree, your statement of -- your position. I have also stated that to the Court earlier, then you mentioned it, so there's no disagreement there. You did not want a unitary state, you did not want a centralised state. You refused to live in that kind of a country, and that's why you started a war to prevent it from happening. Now, on the question of President Sommaruga being misinformed or only partially informed of the situation, that anyone would find very difficult to believe. He had the entire resources of the International Committee of the Red Cross working down there, his people were there. You have cited several times Thierry Germond's comments to us, et cetera, and that's appeared before the Court. So I do not think the ICRC did not going on [sic]. The ICRC is officially charged in the Geneva Conventions with visiting prisoners, whether they're civilians in conflict or military. For example, to this day, the ICRC visits the American Detention Centre at Guantanamo Bay. It is the only organisation permitted to do so. So I find it hard to believe that you say he was misinformed or only partially informed. I think you say that because he was very well informed and said things that are very unpleasant for Bosnian Serbs to hear about their war crimes. I do not agree that my testimony, now or in the Krajisnik case, differ from my contemporary comments and recording of what you and others said. I repeat, it is flattering to be complimented on that point. Nobody has ever challenged my journals, not Milosevic, not Krajisnik. They are accurate. Now, it is also the case that I am not -- as we have pointed out, I am not a court stenographer. Every word that is said is not there; the gist of the meetings are there. And as we said earlier, I often would not report what I said, because I knew what I said and I wasn't interested in having my journals turn into an egoistical exercise. I would never do that. So that, for example, when you do not find in my journals my comment to you already before the war started that you would commit a genocide, I didn't write that down because I know I said it. I didn't believe it at the time, but I know that I said it, and the reason I said it, Dr. Karadzic, is because of your constant emphasis on the genocide of the Serbs during World War II. And that's amply recorded in the journals, including one entry where I note that it was somewhat of a surprise because three minutes passed before you mentioned the Bosnian Serb genocide suffered in the second war. I'm not arguing that point. There was a genocide committed against the Bosnian Serbs. Incidentally, when I once discussed this subject with General Mladic, the very same subject you raised about the Serbs, he said to me that the principal areas where the Bosnian Serbs had suffered the genocide in World War II were Sarajevo, the Sasinska [phoen] Krajina, and Srebrenica. Interesting that he mentioned Srebrenica, in view of what happened later. Dr. Karadzic is the psychiatrist. I am not. It would be interesting to know what was in his mind in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think what you've just seen is a demonstration of what we Americans call filibuster. I wonder if you could give Dr. Karadzic another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was answering his charges, but I'm happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I already was patient about the amount of time cut into my redirect. I don't know how much -- I don't mind the additional five minutes. I don't think it should be due to an alleged filibuster. I think the witness is trying to answer the questions and the issues raised. But I don't want to have no time at all for redirect. There are just a couple of quick issues I think need to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that was the last question. How many more questions do you have, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, as far as this kind of witness is concerned, with such vast experience, one would have to put a great many more questions. However, I'll reduce it to two or three questions and I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, do you agree that what you write contemporaneously is more authentic than what one thinks of that situation 10, 15, or 20 years later? Just yes or no. We can deal with that briefly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You think that our recollections are more accurate and more fresh than at the moment when things actually happen; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's a reason, but if I'm not allowed to state my reason, I simply answer no. I can give you the reason why I say that. That's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you think our recollection is not more fresh and that it is not more accurate 20 years later?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained active in the former Yugoslavia after my period of activity in Bosnia - I've mentioned that - until 1997, so I was fully aware of what was happening at that period. I remained concerned with affairs after 1997. I began my testimony here at this Tribunal in 2001 with Milosevic, so - and I do not say this happily - I have been closely involved with the former Yugoslavia pretty continuously since 1991. And that is why I say, without filibustering, that my recollection is quite good, because it is not just recollection. I've been dealing with the issue for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ambassador, may I ask you -- or, rather, may I infer that what happened was a considerable evolution, in terms of your positions and knowledge? To which extent did your appearance before this Court and your co-operation with the OTP influence the evolution that took place since the period when you recorded these events and when you were there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not influenced at all by the OTP. My appearance before the Court was to tell the truth and the whole truth. I have tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Thank you for everything, especially for your journals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. And I should say at this point, because Dr. Karadzic has mentioned that he has many more questions, that if the Court wishes me to return, I am fully prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very kind of you, Mr. Ambassador. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ambassador. I have just a few moments to raise a couple of quick matters. First of all, with respect to the contention of the accused over the last few moments that there -- that you -- that your testimony in the Krajisnik case about entries in your diary was not reflected in that diary, I'd like to turn to those, so first to the Mitsotakis reference. That concerned testimony in the Krajisnik case beginning at page 4232, 4233, 34, a diary entry of November 23rd, 1992, which can be found at P787, e-court page 68. And Dr. Karadzic pointed out that you testified to hearing from Mitsotakis that Milosevic had said he would accept 45 per cent if it was ethnically clean, and according to Dr. Karadzic, none of that was in your diary. If we could look at the reference at the top left of the screen, which immediately precedes a meeting that begins at 4.35 -- have you found that reference, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you read it -- can you indicate to the Court whether, in fact, the reference you testified to in the Krajisnik case is, indeed, recorded in your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Let me just read it to you. This is Prime Minister Mitsotakis talking to us in November 23rd, 1992, and I quote: "The problem is not percentages on land. Milosevic could live with 45 per cent. He told me so. "What is hard to accept is that Milosevic's segment," meaning the Bosnian Serb segment, "is that Milosevic's segment is not ethnically clean. "But we cannot admit ethnic cleansing in any case." That's Milosevic talking to me and Vance. That's what he said, and that's what I recorded in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. The accused also directed your attention and the Court's attention to testimony in the Krajisnik case which stated: "Tie Serb opstinas to Yugoslavia; otherwise, war will result." And asked you: "Why isn't that in your diary, Mr. Ambassador?" You said you thought it was. Can we turn, please, to P777, e-court page 23, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be the 2nd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe 1991, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1991, I was not in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, December, December.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, December. Excuse me. I apologise to the Court. These note-books are rather heavy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And presumably the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the pages, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you'll find that at page 49, and let me ask you, then, whether or not the reference "Tie Serb opstinas to Yugoslavia; otherwise, war will result," is, indeed, reflected in your diaries.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've just quoted them: "Tie Serb opstinas to Yugoslavia; otherwise, war will result."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now, yesterday there was also an exchange between you and the accused when he asserted -- when he asked whether any of those involved in the negotiations said that he was a liar, asserted that none of them had said that, and also a suggestion by the accused that your position differed from that of your colleagues or those who were at the head of these undertakings and those who assisted you. That was a quote. So in that connection -- oh, and that last remark that I quoted was in connection with an excerpt from the book by Lord Owen, so I'd like to turn to Lord Owen's book and look at excerpts which were not brought to your attention very quickly. First, if we could turn to -- and this is 65 ter 06285. If we could turn to e-court page 186. And looking at the left side of the page, the paragraph that begins: "Ever since I had clashed with Karadzic in Banja Luka over ethnic cleansing in September 1992 ..." That passage goes on to note Mr. Karadzic's excuses for ethnic cleansing and the fact that he didn't raise any objections to the championing of human rights safe-guards by the negotiations. And then I turn your attention to the last sentence of that paragraph: "All this, however, was a facade to cover up a deep-seated commitment to Serbs not living alongside Muslims and to conducting an ethnic cleansing programme with a bare-faced dishonour of even greater magnitude than his continued inability to respect or even to know the truth." And one more passage, Mr. Ambassador, with time drawing short. That's at page 120 of the e-court. It begins at the top left part of the page, which begins with: "Karadzic's especial skill, and it is a considerable one, is to deflect and defuse a hostile question with an innocent facial expression and apparent concern in his voice." It continues on a question about shelling Sarajevo, and the answer that it's the Muslims who were shelling, and Serbs are just protecting their homes. That paragraph ends with a reference to the fact that Dr. Karadzic's claim that Serbs cannot live together with Muslims and Croats, and not to dump them in the sake sack, like cats and dogs." And, finally, this comment: "Perhaps because we have both trained as physicians, I have found it hard to believe that he could be a practitioner of ethnic cleansing and espouse such an odious philosophy, so totally at odds with the Hippocratic Oath. I initially hoped that there was more respect within the inner man for human life and dignity, but I was doomed to illusion [sic]." Ambassador, very quickly, was Lord Owen one of those persons, in addition to Lord Carrington whom you noted yesterday, one of those involved in the negotiations, who told you that Dr. Karadzic did not tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was deeply disappointed, as he said, with Dr. Karadzic's untruthfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I realise there wasn't much time, I'm already running over, so I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Ambassador Okun, this concludes your evidence. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal yet again and for sharing your experience with us when you worked in Bosnia. This Chamber, and I believe the Tribunal as a whole, very much appreciates your efforts to come here over and over again and help us with our work. I hope that now that your testimony is over, you can relax and enjoy your future endeavours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour, and the Court, and I appreciate all the courtesies that have been shown to me by the Court, the Defendants, and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we can take care of the housekeeping later, but I'll be tendering those excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador, you are now free to go. The part of "Balkan Odyssey" has already been admitted as P799, so I'm wondering what the practice should be, then. The added part will be added to the existing part? We'll deal with it when we resume on Wednesday, Wednesday afternoon. I hope everybody has a good rest until then. We'll rise.
